---
title: "Performance against base R and stringi"
description: >
  How long zuregex takes for common tasks, next to base R's perl = TRUE
  functions and stringi, and what the numbers do and do not show.
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", echo = FALSE)
results <- read.csv("benchmarks.csv")
info <- read.csv("benchmarks-info.csv")
info <- stats::setNames(info$value, info$key)
```

This article compares zuregex with base R's `perl = TRUE` functions and
with [stringi](https://stringi.gagolewski.com/) on eight common tasks. It
is for readers deciding whether the speed difference matters for their
data. The numbers come from one machine. Read them as ratios, not as
times you will see.

## How it was measured

The input is 50,000 synthetic log lines of about 64 ASCII characters.
These are the first two; half the lines have a phone number and half end
in `no phone`.

```
login user id=662153 user447@host6.com beta; warn, call 555-5110
delta beta id=633215 user22@host50.com beta; info, call 555-5676
```

Each task runs the same pattern through the three packages. The script
first checks that all three give the same result, then times each with
`bench::mark()` and keeps the median. One case is a single string, where
the cost of the call itself dominates.

The machine was `r info[["cpu"]]` (`r info[["platform"]]`), running
`r info[["R"]]`, on `r info[["date"]]`. It had zuregex `r info[["zuregex"]]`
with PCRE2 `r info[["pcre2"]]` and its JIT compiler, base R's own PCRE2
`r info[["base_pcre2"]]`, and stringi `r info[["stringi"]]` with ICU
`r info[["icu"]]`. zuregex ran on `r info[["threads"]]` thread.

## Results

Median time per call, in milliseconds. The two right-hand columns say how
many times longer the other package took than zuregex, so a value above 1
means zuregex was faster.

```{r}
w <- stats::reshape(
  results,
  idvar = c("task", "size"),
  timevar = "engine",
  direction = "wide"
)
names(w) <- sub("median_ms.", "", names(w), fixed = TRUE)
table <- data.frame(
  Task = w$task,
  Input = w$size,
  zuregex = w$zuregex,
  `base R` = w$base,
  stringi = w$stringi,
  `base R / zuregex` = w$base / w$zuregex,
  `stringi / zuregex` = w$stringi / w$zuregex,
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(
  table,
  digits = c(0, 0, 3, 3, 3, 1, 1),
  row.names = FALSE,
  align = "llrrrrr"
)
```

The pattern for each task:

| Task | zuregex | base R | stringi |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Detect | `re_detect()` | `grepl()` | `stri_detect_regex()` |
| Count matches | `re_count()` | `gregexpr()`, then counting | `stri_count_regex()` |
| Locate the first match | `re_locate()` | `regexpr()` | `stri_locate_first_regex()` |
| Extract every match | `re_extract_all()` | `gregexpr()` and `regmatches()` | `stri_extract_all_regex()` |
| Capture groups | `re_match()` | `utils::strcapture()` | `stri_match_first_regex()` |
| Replace every match | `re_replace()` | `gsub()` | `stri_replace_all_regex()` |
| Split | `re_split()` | `strsplit()` | `stri_split_regex()` |
| Detect, one string | `re_detect()` | `grepl()` | `stri_detect_regex()` |

## Reading the numbers

The difference from base R is largest where base R needs two steps, a
search and then R code that turns its offsets into counts, strings or
columns: counting, extracting and capturing. `strcapture()` takes both
steps inside one call. zuregex builds those results in C. Where base R also takes one call, as with `grepl()`,
`regexpr()`, `gsub()` and `strsplit()`, the two are much closer.

On a single string the call itself dominates, so the three packages are
within 10 microseconds of each other. zuregex keeps compiled patterns
in a cache, so a pattern used again is not compiled again.

## What the numbers do not show

- **Other machines give other ratios.** The package's own timing tests
  record that `re_detect()` was 0.6 times as fast as `grepl()` on an
  arm64 Mac, and that short calls run 10 to 25% behind base R on Linux,
  where base R's call costs less. The two-step tasks were not measured
  elsewhere.
- **More threads change the large cases.** These results are for one
  thread. On a machine with OpenMP, zuregex matches large inputs on
  several threads; `re_threads()` sets the cap.
- **Patterns differ.** One corpus of short ASCII lines and four patterns
  is a small sample. Time your own patterns on your own data before you
  rely on a ratio.

## Run it yourself

The script is
[`tools/bench/run.R`](https://github.com/pedrobtz/zuregex/blob/main/tools/bench/run.R)
in the source repository. It needs stringi and bench. Run it against an
installed build, because `devtools::load_all()` compiles without
optimisation:

```sh
R CMD INSTALL --preclean --library=/tmp/zr-bench .
Rscript tools/bench/run.R /tmp/zr-bench
```

It writes `vignettes/articles/benchmarks.csv`, which this article reads.

## See also

- [Move from base R and stringr](from-base-r.html) maps each base R function to
  its zuregex verb.
- `?re_threads` and `?re_cache_size` describe the two settings that most
  affect speed.
